name: Yara Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Greenfield Wholesale, which supplies farm stores, pet shops and garden centres across the county. I buy pet food, bird seed, compost and garden sundries, so my year follows the seasons: compost in spring, bird food in autumn. Most days I'm checking stock against last year's weather, talking to about twenty suppliers, and making sure a shop doesn't run out of dog food on a Saturday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the shops. A lot of them are family businesses like my parents' farm shop out on the Hollow Lane, and I know how much a late delivery hurts them. What wears me out is the weather, honestly, one wet spring and I'm sitting on two thousand bags of compost. I've started using the AI that came with our ordering system now and then to check my forecasts, but I still go with my own judgement most of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just another tool, like the calculator was. At work I'd say let's not get carried away. I'm not much online, maybe the school parents' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the AI part suits me fine, the job is still about knowing the shops and the seasons. What's on my mind is Dad. My dad had a heart scare in the summer, and my mum can't run the farm shop on her own. And Greenfield had a poor year after the wet spring, so there's no pay rise this year for any of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI forecast in our ordering system as a second opinion, nothing more. I'd keep doing Saturdays at the farm shop, and probably some Sunday mornings now, so Dad can rest. Kenji and I would put the new garden fence off until next year and keep the hundred a month going into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about computers, about Dad, and about how many weekends one person has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you go with your own judgement most of the time. When has that paid off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last autumn the system said order the usual bird seed, but I'd heard from three shops that people were feeding more birds because of a cold snap. I ordered a third extra and we sold every bag by December. The shopkeepers knew about the cold snap before any computer did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your dad couldn't work at all, what would happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would want me there more, and I'd have to choose between Greenfield's wage and the shop. We couldn't live on what the shop pays, not with the mortgage and about three months of savings. So I'd do both and be tired, and Kenji would pick up more with Aiko and Ren.

S0.say: I'd say AI is just another tool, like the calculator was, and that we shouldn't get carried away. I'm hardly online, maybe the school parents' group.
S0.think: The AI part suits me, because the job is still about knowing shops and seasons. What worries me is Dad's heart scare, Mum not managing the farm shop alone, and no pay rise at Greenfield after a poor year.
S0.do: Keeps using the ordering system's AI forecast as a second opinion. Works Saturdays and now some Sunday mornings at the farm shop so her dad can rest, and puts off the garden fence while keeping 100 a month going into savings.
S0.feel: Uneasy, not about computers but about her father's health and how many weekends she can give.
S0.quote: My dad had a heart scare in the summer, and my mum can't run the farm shop on her own.
S0.fieldNote: AI barely registers for Yara here; her unease comes from her father's health, a pay freeze after a wet spring and stretched weekends. She can't afford to swap Greenfield's wage for the shop, so she would simply do both. Her trust in shopkeepers over software shows in the bird seed story.

steps.text: Use the ordering system's AI forecast as a second opinion
Work Saturdays and some Sundays at her parents' farm shop
Put off the new garden fence until next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes and you get on with it, the way farmers always have. At work I'd say I'm happy to learn the new ways once they're working. I wouldn't join any online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Most of my job is forecasting and ordering, and that's the buying the card says computers take over. Greenfield has five buyers, and I could see them needing three, so my parents' farm shop stops being a hobby and starts being a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I saw the others getting good results, I'd ask my manager, Gareth, to train me properly on the AI ordering. I'd put an extra hundred a month into savings, which means fewer meals out. And I'd sit down with Dad about the shop paying me properly for Saturdays and building up its own deliveries, so there's a second wage growing in case Greenfield lets me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A cloud I'd carry to work every day, though I've got somewhere to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see others get results. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen new systems come in and cause chaos, like the time the stock screen double-ordered compost one spring. I'd rather learn from someone else's mistakes with a new computer system. Once the system is proven, I'll be right there, but I know waiting too long could cost me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for help anywhere outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. Kenji's an electrician at the bottling factory, so his work is steady and it's hands-on. I wouldn't go to the government unless there was really nothing else.

S1.say: I'd say change comes and you get on with it, the way farmers always have, and that I'm happy to learn new ways once they work. I'd stay out of online arguments.
S1.think: Most of my job is forecasting and ordering, exactly the buying the computers take over. Greenfield could go from five buyers to three, so the farm shop stops being a hobby and becomes a plan.
S1.do: Asks Gareth for proper AI ordering training once colleagues show good results, and saves an extra 100 a month by cutting meals out. Agrees with her dad that the farm shop pays her properly for Saturdays and starts its own deliveries, as a second wage in case Greenfield lets her go.
S1.feel: Anxious, carrying a daily cloud to work, but steadied by having the farm shop and Kenji's steady wage.
S1.quote: Greenfield has five buyers, and I could see them needing three, so my parents' farm shop stops being a hobby and starts being a plan.
S1.fieldNote: Yara expects Greenfield's buying team to shrink and knows she could be one of those cut, which moves her from background worry to real planning. Her caution with new systems hasn't changed, but she admits waiting too long could cost her. The farm shop and Kenji's hands-on job give her more footing than most.

steps.text: Ask Gareth for AI ordering training once colleagues show results
Save an extra 100 a month by cutting meals out
Get paid properly for Saturdays at the farm shop
Start local deliveries from the farm shop with her dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast, and the people building it should have thought about families. At work I'd say we need honest answers about jobs. At church we'd talk about looking after one another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my buying job is gone within a year or two of 2028. But I'm luckier than most, because my parents' farm shop is real, physical work, and Kenji is an electrician, so he has the extra three years before the robots. We wouldn't be on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents straight away about working at the farm shop properly, maybe taking it over as Dad wants to slow down. We'd cut back: no holiday, no new fence, cheaper food shopping. I'd stay at Greenfield as long as they'd keep me, and move to the shop when the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Shaken, but with somewhere to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A farm shop is a big pay drop from a buyer's salary, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, maybe half in the first years. But we'd have Kenji's wage, and I know how to buy for a shop better than anyone, it's what I do all day. I've spent fifteen years buying for other people's shops, so I might as well buy for my own family's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Aiko and Ren that their mother is going to work at Grandma's shop, and they can help on Saturdays. They'd think it's a treat. I'd keep the worry for Kenji and me.

S2.say: I'd say it's far too fast and the people building it should have thought about families. I'd want honest answers at work, and at church we'd talk about looking after one another.
S2.think: My buying job is gone within a year or two of 2028, but I'm luckier than most. My parents' farm shop is hands-on work, and my husband's electrician job has three extra years before robots.
S2.do: Talks to her parents at once about working in and perhaps taking over the farm shop. Cuts the holiday, the new fence and the food bill, and stays at Greenfield until the job ends.
S2.feel: Anxious and shaken, but with somewhere to stand.
S2.quote: I've spent fifteen years buying for other people's shops, so I might as well buy for my own family's shop.
S2.fieldNote: Yara's family farm shop changes everything for her: it gives her a hands-on fallback that thinking AI can't take straight away. Her traditional values show in turning to family first and keeping the worry from the children. She is shaken but not cornered.

steps.text: Ask her parents about working in and taking over the farm shop
Cancel the holiday and the new fence and shop cheaper
Move to the farm shop when the Greenfield job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and families should use it to get their house in order. At work I'd suggest we plan properly. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I had time. The buying job probably goes around 2031, and I'd be 48. With five years I could build up the farm shop on the side so it's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI ordering at Greenfield properly, once it's proven, because it would help at the farm shop too. I'd spend Saturdays building the shop's online orders and local deliveries with Dad. We'd put an extra hundred and fifty a month aside to get to six months of savings by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a plan. Like knowing the harvest will be hard but the barn's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the AI so you could use it in the farm shop. Isn't that the same AI taking your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and that's a funny thing to admit. But if it's coming anyway, I'd rather it works for my family than against me. My dad would grumble about it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots three years later? Does the farm shop survive those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I wouldn't pretend to. People like buying eggs and honey from a person they know. A robot can stack the shelves, but I don't think people will drive out to Hollow Lane to buy honey from a robot.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and families should get their house in order. I'd suggest planning at work and say the same at church.
S3.think: I'd feel I had time: the buying job probably goes around 2031, when I'd be 48, and I could build up the farm shop on the side.
S3.do: Learns Greenfield's AI ordering once proven, to use it in the farm shop too. Spends Saturdays building the shop's online orders and local deliveries, and saves an extra hundred and fifty a month towards six months by 2030.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a plan, like a hard harvest ahead with the barn ready.
S3.quote: A robot can stack the shelves, but I don't think people will drive out to Hollow Lane to buy honey from a robot.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Yara turns the farm shop into a side project she builds with her father. She sees the irony of learning the AI that replaces her and uses it for her family's business. She is honest that she doesn't know if robots will reach the shop.

steps.text: Learn the AI ordering system once it's proven
Build online orders and deliveries for the farm shop on Saturdays
Save an extra hundred and fifty a month until 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and there's no sense worrying now. Work hard, save, look after your family. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd feel quite manageable. I'd be 53 when AGI arrives, Dad would be ready to hand over the farm shop, and the mortgage would be mostly paid. It almost fits too neatly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Greenfield and pick up the AI tools as they become normal. Over a few years, Kenji and I would put some savings into the farm shop, maybe a new chiller and a delivery van. We'd also talk to the children about their studies, nothing that's all screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it fits too neatly. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's health, for one, he's seventy-one. And whether people still have money to spend at farm shops if half the county loses office jobs in 2036. I can't plan for everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Aiko about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aiko is eleven and wants to be a vet, which I'd be glad about. A vet has to put their hands on a sick animal, and I think vets will need hands for a long time.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and there's no sense worrying now: work hard, save and look after your family.
S4.think: It'd feel manageable: I'd be 53, my father ready to hand over the farm shop and the mortgage mostly paid. It almost fits too neatly.
S4.do: Carries on at Greenfield, picking up AI tools as they become normal. Puts savings into a new chiller and delivery van for the family farm shop, and steers the children away from screen-only studies.
S4.quote: A vet has to put their hands on a sick animal, and I think vets will need hands for a long time.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Yara's plans line up almost perfectly with her family's farm shop and the mortgage end date. Her worries are her father's health and local spending, not her own job. She welcomes her daughter's hands-on career choice.

steps.text: Pick up the AI tools at Greenfield as they become normal
Put savings into a chiller and delivery van for the farm shop
Steer both children away from screen-only studies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Even with the farm shop, two years is very fast, and a lot of people I know haven't got a family shop to fall back on. What would help is apprenticeships and small business help, so people can learn a trade or build something, rather than just a payment in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the small shops we supply. If the big distributors use AI to cut prices, the family shops will struggle too. When a family shop closes, a whole village loses the place where people still talk to each other.

headlineQuote: When a family shop closes, a whole village loses the place where people still talk to each other.
portrait: Yara Ito, 43, buys pet food, bird seed and garden supplies for Greenfield Wholesale, which serves farm stores, pet shops and garden centres. She uses AI now and then as a second opinion but trusts what shopkeepers tell her. Even if AI stalls she is uneasy, worried about her father's heart and a pay freeze, and under steady change she is anxious, expecting five buyers to become three and turning her parents' farm shop on Hollow Lane into a real plan. That shop is her fallback in every AGI picture, so AGI by 2028 makes her anxious rather than desperate, and with more time she builds it up and grows calmer. Traditional at heart, she turns to family first and wants apprenticeships and small business help rather than payments.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years is very fast even with the farm shop, and many people she knows have no family business to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and small business help so people can learn a trade or build something, rather than just a payment in the post.
